Overcoming the Main Challenges

Problem: Naive Splitting

  • Splitting by game gave only 200 val samples from 2 games — too small and unrepresentative
  • Random splitting could place an original frame in train and its augmented variant in val — the model memorizes instead of learning
  • Result: 95% train vs 72% val accuracy

Solution: Frame-Group Split

  • Group by (game_id, frame) — each frame and all its augmented variants go to the same split
  • 20% of frame-groups held for validation → 595 boards from 9 games
  • Result: balanced, representative validation with no data leakage

Problem: Occlusions (No Labels)

  • Hands and arms block squares during play
  • No occlusion labels in the original dataset

Solution: Dual Defense

  • Manual tagging - built an interactive tool to label occluded squares per frame
  • OOD detection - if the model isn't confident enough, it flags the square as occluded

Robustness

Offline Augmentation x5 data

4 pre-generated variants per game to simulate different conditions

Online Augmentation per square

Mild transforms during training: ColorJitter, ±5° rotation, GaussianBlur, RandomErasing

EfficientNet-B2

Best accuracy-to-parameter ratio for our data size. Outperformed ResNet18 (+5.96%) and larger models that overfit.

CrossEntropy Loss

Label smoothing (0.1) + inverse-frequency class weights for rare pieces

Occlusion Handling

Supervised occlusion class (13) + confidence thresholding + temperature scaling

Why It Works

Prevents catastrophic forgetting. Head stabilizes on stable features first, then full fine-tuning adapts the backbone.

Strengths

  • Rooks (96-99%): distinctive castle shape
  • Pawns (95%+): abundant, consistent shape
  • Overfit gap: -0.62% (val > train)

Weaknesses

  • Queens (~91%): confused with rooks/bishops
  • Occluded (87%): inherently ambiguous

Ablation Study

What Didn't Work

ResNet-18 Backbone

Too weak for fine-grained piece classification. EfficientNet-B2 gave +6% accuracy.

Full Fine-Tuning from Start

Catastrophic forgetting destroyed ImageNet features. 95% train vs 72% val.

Heavy Augmentation

Strong ColorJitter overlapped with offline variants, creating unrealistic images. Reducing to mild values improved results.

Higher Dropout (0.4)

Reduced model capacity without enough regularization benefit. Reverting to 0.3 with gradual unfreezing worked better.

Key Takeaways

1

Data Quality > Model Complexity

Proper split and augmentation contributed more than any architecture change

2

Gradual Unfreezing is Key

Stabilize the head, then fine-tune everything - prevents catastrophic forgetting (+4%)

3

Right-Sized Models Win

With limited data, inductive bias matters more than raw capacity

How It Works

python predict.py --image board.jpg

  • Takes a single RGB image as input
  • Returns an 8×8 tensor with class IDs (0-13)
  • Saves a chess diagram SVG to ./results/
  • Occluded squares marked with red X
